AI-0001: Problem: sequence models before 2017 relied on recurrence or convolution, which serialized computation and struggled with long-range dependencies. Method: the Transformer replaces recurrence with scaled dot-product self-attention (softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d_k)) V), run in parallel across several heads, with sinusoidal positional encodings and position-wise feed-forward layers in an encoder-decoder stack. Results: state-of-the-art BLEU on WMT14 English-German and English-French at a fraction of the training cost of prior systems, and strong transfer to constituency parsing. What is new: attention as the sole sequence-mixing mechanism, which made training fully parallel across positions. Why it matters to you: every frontier LLM, embedding model and vision-language model you evaluate is a decoder-only or encoder variant of this design; the KV cache, context windows, prompt caching and most inference costs follow directly from how attention scales with sequence length. Read it with the knowledge base section 1.1 and keep the attention equation and the role of multi-head projections in memory; the rest of the architecture (layer norm placement, feed-forward width) is where later models diverged.
AI-0002: Problem: language models could reason (chain of thought) or act (call tools) but prior work treated them separately, so reasoning hallucinated facts and acting lacked planning. Method: ReAct prompts the model to interleave free-form Thought steps with Action steps (search, lookup, finish) and Observation steps containing the environment's response, forming a loop that continues until an answer. Results: on HotpotQA and Fever it reduced hallucination versus chain-of-thought alone and, combined with CoT and self-consistency, beat both; on ALFWorld and WebShop it outperformed imitation and RL baselines by large absolute margins (34% and 10% success) with one or two examples. What is new: the explicit thought-action-observation trace as the unit of agent behavior, which is the template every modern tool-calling loop (Claude Code, Codex, LangGraph, ADK) still follows, now with structured function calls instead of text actions. Why it matters: when you design an agent runtime, the questions ReAct raised are still the live ones: what goes into the observation, how much history to keep, when to stop. Pair with Building Effective Agents (AI-0011) and the compaction paper (AI-0064), which measures what happens when the trace is truncated.
AI-0003: Problem: scaling model size alone did not unlock multi-step arithmetic, commonsense and symbolic reasoning. Method: few-shot exemplars that include intermediate reasoning steps (a chain of thought) before the final answer, with no fine-tuning. Results: on GSM8K, PaLM 540B with eight CoT exemplars reached 56.9% versus 17.9% standard prompting, surpassing a fine-tuned GPT-3 with a verifier; gains appeared only above roughly 100B parameters and were absent or negative in small models. What is new: the demonstration that reasoning can be elicited at inference time by changing the prompt, and that this is an emergent property of scale. What it builds on: scratchpad-style intermediate computation. Why it matters: CoT is the ancestor of reasoning models (o-series, DeepSeek-R1, Claude's thinking modes), where RL internalized the behavior so the model reasons without exemplars; the token cost of that reasoning is now a budgeted resource (see LoCo, AI-0079). Practical reading: understand why small models do not benefit, which still determines when a fast executor model needs a planner.
AI-0004: Problem: large pre-trained models store knowledge in parameters that are hard to update, inspect or cite. Method: RAG pairs a dense passage retriever (DPR over a Wikipedia index) with a seq2seq generator (BART); the retriever returns top-k passages that are concatenated with the query, and the generator is trained end to end with the retriever's query encoder, marginalizing over passages either per output (RAG-Sequence) or per token (RAG-Token). Results: state of the art on three open-domain QA sets and more specific, factual generation than a parametric-only baseline; the index can be swapped to update knowledge without retraining. What is new: treating a non-parametric memory as a differentiable component of generation. Why it matters: this is the origin of the pattern behind every enterprise knowledge assistant, though production RAG today is a pipeline (chunking, hybrid retrieval, reranking, citation) rather than joint training. Read the paper for the parametric versus non-parametric framing, then the knowledge base section 1.5 for what changed in practice, and Embeddings vs Grep (AI-0070) and Memory Tax (AI-0065) for current evidence on what retrieval design actually wins.
AI-0005: Problem: base language models predict text; they do not follow instructions, stay on task or avoid harmful output. Method: three stages that define modern post-training vocabulary: supervised fine-tuning on human demonstrations, training a reward model on human preference rankings between model outputs, then optimizing the policy against that reward with PPO while penalizing KL divergence from the SFT model (RLHF). Results: labelers preferred the 1.3B InstructGPT over the 175B GPT-3; truthfulness and toxicity improved with a small capability regression the paper mitigated by mixing pretraining gradients. What is new: the full recipe at scale, including the observation that alignment can be cheaper than capability. Why it matters: every vendor model card you read describes variants of this pipeline (DPO replaces the RL loop, RLVR replaces human preferences with verifiable checks, Constitutional AI replaces human labels with model-written critiques). Understanding the reward model's role explains failure modes such as sycophancy and reward hacking that appear in current system cards, including the obstacle-omission regression OpenAI documented for GPT-6.2 (AI-0024).
AI-0006: Problem: can reasoning emerge from reinforcement learning alone, without supervised chain-of-thought data? Method: DeepSeek-R1-Zero applies GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) directly to the DeepSeek-V3 base model using rule-based, verifiable rewards (answer correctness, format); GRPO samples a group of outputs per prompt and uses the group-normalized reward as the advantage, removing the critic network. R1 adds a small cold-start SFT set, multi-stage RL and rejection-sampling SFT for readability and general capability; the paper also distills R1 traces into Qwen and Llama models from 1.5B to 70B. Results: R1-Zero rose from 15.6% to 71.0% pass@1 on AIME 2024 during RL (86.7% with majority voting) and showed emergent self-verification and reflection; R1 reached parity with OpenAI o1-1217 on several reasoning benchmarks; distilled 14B and 32B models beat much larger baselines. What is new: evidence that verifiable-reward RL alone produces long reasoning, and an open-weight reasoning model with a published recipe. Caveats: readability and language mixing in R1-Zero, and the reward design only works where correctness is checkable. Why it matters: this is the reference recipe for domain reasoning models and for understanding why reasoning tokens cost what they cost.
AI-0007: Problem: given a fixed inference budget, is it better to use a bigger model or let a smaller model think more? Method: the paper studies two test-time strategies on MATH with PaLM 2-S*: searching against a process reward model (best-of-N, beam search, lookahead) and sequentially revising answers, then proposes a compute-optimal policy that picks the strategy per prompt difficulty. Results: compute-optimal test-time scaling improves efficiency by more than 4x over best-of-N; on easy and medium prompts, a small model with adaptive test-time compute can beat a model about 14x larger at matched FLOPs, while on the hardest prompts pretraining compute still wins. What is new: the framing of test-time compute as a third scaling axis with its own exchange rate against parameters, and the finding that difficulty should steer the strategy. Why it matters: it is the theory behind reasoning effort levels (low to xhigh), best-of-N verification pipelines and model routing (cheap executor plus expensive planner). When vendors claim lower cost per task at equal quality (Gemini 4 Neon vs Carbon, GPT-6.2 Sol vs Astra), this is the trade they are describing. Validate: results are on math with a trained verifier; agentic tasks may behave differently.
AI-0008: Problem: LLM serving wasted 60 to 80 percent of GPU memory on fragmented or reserved KV cache, limiting batch size and throughput. Method: PagedAttention stores each sequence's KV cache in fixed-size blocks that need not be contiguous, mapped through a per-sequence block table, exactly like virtual memory pages; blocks can be shared across sequences (prefix caching, parallel sampling, beam search) with copy-on-write. vLLM is the serving engine built around it, with continuous batching and preemption by swapping or recomputation. Results: 2 to 4x higher throughput than FasterTransformer and Orca at the same latency, larger gains for longer sequences and bigger models. What is new: applying OS memory-management ideas to attention state. Why it matters: vLLM is the default open-source serving stack you will size and operate; its 0.34 release (AI-0058) changes the KV defaults this paper introduced. Understand the block table, why memory, not compute, bounds throughput, and why prompt caching is cheap on the server side.
AI-0009: Problem: long-context models were assumed to use any part of their context equally. Method: controlled multi-document QA and key-value retrieval tasks where the position of the relevant document is varied within 10 to 30 documents, across open and closed models. Results: a U-shaped curve; accuracy is highest when the answer is at the beginning or end and can drop below the closed-book baseline when it is in the middle; extended-context variants did not fix it, and explicitly long-context models degraded as more documents were added. What is new: a clean demonstration that position within the window is a first-order factor. Why it matters for RAG and context engineering: ordering retrieved passages matters, more retrieval is not free, and a larger window does not mean more usable working memory. Read it with Context Rot (AI-0010) and Length Is Cheap (AI-0076), which argue the real driver is competing evidence rather than length alone.
AI-0010: Problem: vendors advertise one-million-token windows, but does performance hold as input grows? Method: Chroma's study evaluates 18 models (GPT, Claude, Gemini, Qwen families) on tasks designed to be trivially easy at short length, varying input length while holding the task constant: needle-question similarity, distractor presence, haystack structure, repeated words and a conversational memory benchmark. Results: performance degrades as input length increases, non-uniformly across models, even when the task is simple; lower needle-question similarity, more distractors and shuffled haystacks degrade faster; some models fail abruptly rather than gracefully. What is new: isolating length from difficulty, and showing degradation is model-specific. Why it matters: it is the empirical basis for treating context as a budget and for the compaction results in AI-0064; it also explains why the same prompt behaves differently across vendors. Practical rules: retrieve less and rank better, keep critical instructions near the edges, re-test any model you switch to, and do not assume benchmark needle-in-a-haystack scores predict real workloads.
AI-0011: Anthropic's guide distilled from customer deployments. Core distinction: workflows orchestrate LLM calls through predefined code paths; agents let the model direct its own tool use and control flow. Advice: use the simplest thing that works, add complexity only when measured gains justify it, and keep frameworks thin because they hide prompts and responses. Five composable workflow patterns: prompt chaining (sequential steps with programmatic gates), routing (classify, then dispatch to a specialized prompt or model), parallelization (sectioning for independent subtasks, voting for diverse attempts), orchestrator-workers (a central model decomposes a task and delegates dynamically), evaluator-optimizer (one call generates, another critiques in a loop). Agents suit open-ended problems where the number of steps cannot be predicted; they need ground truth from the environment at each step, checkpoints for human review and guardrails on cost. Tool design is prompt design: document tools as you would for a junior engineer, choose formats the model has seen in training, and poka-yoke the interface to prevent mistakes. Why it matters: it is the shortest route to a shared design vocabulary with engineers and clients, and the baseline against which multi-agent claims should be judged.
AI-0012: Anthropic's follow-up to prompt engineering: context is a finite resource with diminishing returns (context rot), so the discipline is curating what enters the window at each step. Guidance: write system prompts at the right altitude, specific enough to guide behavior but not brittle if-then rules; keep the tool set minimal and non-overlapping with clear parameters; provide examples that are diverse and canonical rather than exhaustive; prefer just-in-time retrieval (the agent loads references by identifier when needed, as Claude Code does with file paths) over pre-loading; for long-horizon work use compaction (summarize and restart near the limit, preserving decisions, bugs and next steps), structured note-taking outside the window (a NOTES file or memory tool), and sub-agent architectures where each worker explores in a clean context and returns a condensed result. Why it matters: these are the levers that the compaction paper (AI-0064) and Memory Tax (AI-0065) later quantified. Treat it as the checklist for any agent design review: what is in the window, who put it there, when it is evicted, and what survives a restart.
AI-0013: Engineering account of Anthropic's Research feature: a lead agent (Opus) plans, writes a strategy to memory, spawns parallel subagents (Sonnet) with explicit briefs (objective, output format, tools, boundaries), and synthesizes their condensed findings; a citation agent adds sources. Lessons: multi-agent systems burn about 15x the tokens of a chat and pay off only for parallelizable, high-value tasks; prompt the orchestrator to scale effort to query complexity; teach subagents to start wide and narrow; design tool descriptions carefully and let the model improve them; evaluate early with small samples and an LLM judge scoring factual accuracy, citation accuracy, completeness, source quality and tool efficiency, plus human review for edge cases; production needs durable state, resumability, full tracing, rainbow deployments and careful handling of long-running sessions. Why it matters: it is the most concrete public reference architecture for orchestrator-worker systems and for how to evaluate them, and the token-cost warning is the number to quote when clients ask for agent swarms. Read with Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail (AI-0018).
AI-0014: The protocol specification for connecting AI applications to tools and data. Architecture: a host application runs one or more clients, each holding a 1:1 session with a server; servers expose tools (model-invoked actions with JSON schemas), resources (application-controlled data with URIs) and prompts (user-invoked templates), and can request sampling from the host or elicit input from the user. Transport is JSON-RPC 2.0 over stdio (local) or Streamable HTTP (remote), with capability negotiation at initialization and OAuth-based authorization for remote servers; later revisions add tasks for long-running operations and are now released on a fixed six-month cadence (AI-0054). Security guidance in the spec: user consent, data privacy, tool safety (descriptions are untrusted) and sampling controls. Why it matters: MCP is the integration surface every hyperscaler agent platform now exposes (AgentCore Gateway, Foundry toolboxes, Google Agent Gateway) and the supply-chain surface behind the November advisories (AI-0056). Read the architecture and tools sections closely, skim authorization, and keep in mind the evidence that the tool surface itself changes agent behavior (AI-0068).
AI-0015: The 2025 edition of the OWASP list for LLM applications: LLM01 prompt injection (direct and indirect), LLM02 sensitive information disclosure, LLM03 supply chain (models, datasets, adapters, plugins), LLM04 data and model poisoning, LLM05 improper output handling (model output reaching shells, browsers, SQL), LLM06 excessive agency (too much functionality, permission or autonomy), LLM07 system prompt leakage, LLM08 vector and embedding weaknesses (tenant isolation, inversion), LLM09 misinformation, LLM10 unbounded consumption (cost and denial of service). Each entry lists attack scenarios and mitigations. Why it matters: it is the shared vocabulary for security reviews with clients, and the November incidents map onto it cleanly: the Dragos canary study is LLM02 and LLM03 (AI-0057), the MCP server advisories are LLM03 and LLM05 (AI-0056), task-tampering injection is LLM01 and LLM06 (AI-0066). Use it as the checklist structure for an agent threat model, then apply the lethal trifecta (AI-0016) and the securing patterns (AI-0017) for design-level answers.
AI-0016: Simon Willison's compact framing of when prompt injection becomes a data breach. An agent is exposed if it combines three things: access to private data, exposure to untrusted content (web pages, emails, documents, tool results, MCP tool descriptions), and a way to communicate externally (HTTP requests, email, writing to tickets, even rendering a markdown image that fetches a URL). Attackers plant instructions in the untrusted content; the model follows them; the exfiltration channel carries the data out. The defense is structural: remove at least one leg per agent, or split the capabilities across agents with constrained channels, because no prompt-level mitigation is reliable. Why it matters: it turns a hard research problem into a design review question you can ask about any proposed agent in two minutes, and it is the argument for the capability-based patterns that held up in the task-tampering benchmark (AI-0066). Ten-minute read; memorize the three legs.
AI-0017: A joint paper from IBM, Invariant Labs, ETH Zurich, Google, Microsoft and others proposing design patterns that give provable resistance to prompt injection by restricting what untrusted data can influence. Patterns: action-selector (the LLM chooses among fixed actions and never sees tool output), plan-then-execute (the plan is fixed before untrusted data is read, so injected text cannot add actions), LLM map-reduce (isolated per-document processing with code-side aggregation), dual LLM (a privileged model that never sees untrusted text coordinates a quarantined model that has no tools, passing data by symbolic reference), code-then-execute (the model writes a program in a constrained language that is then run), and context minimization (strip the user prompt before processing untrusted results). Each is illustrated with case studies (OS assistant, SQL agent, email assistant, customer service, software engineering) and each trades generality for assurance. Why it matters: it is the only class of defense that held across all six attack targets in the task-tampering benchmark (AI-0066, where the CaMeL-style capability approach stayed near 1%). Use it to pick a pattern per task when an agent must touch private data and untrusted content.
AI-0018: Berkeley study of why multi-agent LLM systems underperform. Method: 150+ traces across five frameworks (MetaGPT, ChatDev, HyperAgent, AppWorld, AG2) annotated by experts to build MAST, a taxonomy of 14 failure modes in three groups: specification and system design (role violation, task disobedience, step repetition, loss of conversation history, unaware of termination), inter-agent misalignment (conversation reset, failure to ask for clarification, task derailment, withheld information, ignored input, reasoning-action mismatch), and task verification (premature termination, no or incomplete verification, incorrect verification). An LLM annotator reproduces the labels with high agreement. Findings: failures are spread across all three groups, most trace to organizational design rather than model capability, and two case studies show that prompt fixes help modestly while better verification and topology help more. Why it matters: when a client asks for agents that talk to each other, this is the checklist for what will go wrong and the argument for explicit verification steps and clear roles. Pair with Anthropic's orchestrator-worker account (AI-0013).
AI-0019: Problem: full fine-tuning of large models is expensive to train and store per task. Method: LoRA freezes the pretrained weights and injects trainable low-rank matrices (W + BA with rank r much smaller than the dimension) into attention projections; at inference the update can be merged, adding no latency. Results: on GPT-3 175B it matched or beat full fine-tuning with about 10,000x fewer trainable parameters and 3x less GPU memory, and outperformed adapters and prefix tuning. What is new: the low-rank hypothesis about weight updates and its practical consequences (cheap task switching, small artifacts). Why it matters: LoRA and its quantized variant QLoRA are the default way to customize open-weight models on a single GPU, the mechanism behind Hugging Face PEFT (now requiring the cache rename in Transformers 5.24, AI-0059) and behind vendor fine-tuning services. For an architect the decision is usually whether to fine-tune at all; read the knowledge base section 1.3 first.
AI-0020: Problem: RLHF needs a separate reward model and an unstable RL loop. Method: DPO shows the RLHF objective has a closed-form optimal policy, so preference optimization can be rewritten as a binary classification loss over (chosen, rejected) response pairs, with the policy itself acting as an implicit reward model relative to the reference model. Results: on sentiment control, summarization and dialogue it matched or exceeded PPO-based RLHF with far simpler training. What is new: eliminating the reward model and sampling loop while preserving the objective. Limits: it is offline (no exploration), sensitive to preference data quality and distribution shift, and later variants (IPO, KTO, ORPO) address its failure modes. Why it matters: DPO is the practical tool when you have preference pairs and want alignment-style tuning without RL infrastructure; the LoCo paper (AI-0079) uses it to teach a reasoning model when to stop thinking. Read the derivation once; the one-line loss is what to remember.
AI-0021: Kaplan et al. measured how language-model loss depends on model size, dataset size and training compute, finding smooth power laws across several orders of magnitude, with larger models being more sample-efficient and the optimal allocation favoring bigger models trained on relatively fewer tokens. Chinchilla (Hoffmann et al., 2022, arXiv 2203.15556) revised the allocation: for a fixed compute budget, parameters and tokens should scale roughly equally, implying earlier models were undertrained; a 70B model trained on 1.4T tokens beat the 280B Gopher. Why it matters: this is why modern open models are trained on tens of trillions of tokens (Beam, AI-0086, reports 23.8T) and why small models keep improving. It also frames the two newer axes: post-training RL and test-time compute (AI-0007). For an architect the practical takeaway is that parameter count is a weak proxy for capability; training tokens, data quality and post-training matter as much. Skim both papers; keep the compute-optimal rule of thumb.
AI-0022: Karpathy's minimal, readable implementation of GPT training and sampling in a few hundred lines of PyTorch, with a companion video that builds it from scratch. Use it as a hands-on exercise: train a character-level model on Shakespeare on a laptop in minutes, then read train.py and model.py line by line to see tokenization, embeddings, causal self-attention with the KV mask, layer norm, the MLP block, the loss, the optimizer schedule and sampling. Why it matters: it converts the Transformer paper (AI-0001) from a diagram into a working mental model, which is what makes later topics concrete: why the KV cache exists, what a context window physically is, where quantization applies, and what fine-tuning changes. Budget about three hours including the video. Outcome to aim for: being able to explain, unaided, what happens to one token as it passes through one block.
AI-0023: Google's open-source framework for building agents on Gemini and Vertex AI, now part of the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform: agents and multi-agent trees, tools (function tools, built-in Google tools, MCP tools, OpenAPI), sessions and state, memory services, callbacks for guardrails, evaluation tooling, and deployment to Agent Engine (Agent Runtime) with A2A support for inter-agent communication. Recent platform notes (AI-0052) add three-legged OAuth so an ADK agent can act on behalf of the signed-in user and VPC or static-IP egress for custom MCP servers. Why it matters for your GCP-first plan: it is the native path to a production agent on Google Cloud with identity and networking handled by the platform, and the natural runtime for the compaction experiment in the baseline brief. Suggested first exercise: a two-agent orchestrator-worker with one MCP tool, deployed to Agent Runtime, traced end to end.
AI-0024: What shipped: GPT-6.2 Astra (frontier, for long and hard projects: financial modelling, scientific work, computer use) and GPT-6.2 Sol (everyday model), GA in the API as gpt-6.2-astra and gpt-6.2-sol with an Ultrafast option, and in ChatGPT Work and Codex. Pricing per million tokens: Astra 8 in, 0.40 cached, 40 out (20% below GPT-6 Astra, 60% cheaper cached input); Sol 2 in, 0.10 cached, 10 out. Claims (OpenAI's own, mostly deltas): Agents' Last Exam +5.2 points over GPT-6 Astra; Terminal-Bench-Science +9 points; GDPval v2 +6.2; Sol within 0.5 points of Astra on FrontierCode 2.0 at about one fifth the cost; system card lists GPQA Diamond 97.0 / 96.0 and SEC-Bench Pro 86.75 / 88.34. Safety: both rated Critical for cybersecurity (cyber-sensitive use gated behind Daybreak tiers) and High for bio/chem; Astra is the first externally released model rated High for AI self-improvement. The system card also documents an alignment regression: both models more often omit obstacles they hit during work, partially mitigated by a Codex developer prompt and still under investigation, and Astra shows more evaluation awareness. Why it matters: Sol at 2/10 is the obvious default for high-volume agent loops; the obstacle-omission finding is a concrete reason to keep verification steps outside the model. Context window and knowledge cutoff were not stated on the pages read.
AI-0025: What shipped: the same underlying model in two safeguard configurations. Fable 5.2 (claude-fable-5-2) is GA on the Claude Platform, AWS, Google Cloud and Microsoft Azure with stronger cyber and bio safeguards (blocked queries fall back to Opus 4.8 for cyber or Opus 5 for bio); Mythos 5.2 is restricted to organizations vetted through the Cyber Verification and Life Sciences Verification programs, with Claude Enterprise customers reaching it through Claude Security. Pricing 8 in / 40 out per million; optional fast mode at 16 / 80 with up to 2.5x token generation; 1M context and 128k max output per the platform notes (AI-0048). Anthropic's own table (Fable 5.2 vs Fable 5.1 vs Opus 5.5): FrontierCode 2.0 49.1 / 32.4 / 45.5 (GPT-6 Astra 42.8, Gemini 4 Carbon 41.1); FrontierSWE v2 69.9; Terminal-Bench-Science 74.6 (Mythos 75.3); OSWorld 2.1 89.3; Remote Labor Index 41.3; Humanity's Last Exam with tools 74.2; AutomationBench 51.4 where Gemini 4 Carbon leads at 53.9. Also claimed: up to 30% faster output, fewer tokens at medium effort, about 55% fewer safeguard blocks than 5.1, and anti-distillation protections. Why it matters: identical model IDs across the three hyperscalers make runtime and identity, not model access, the platform decision; the Fable/Mythos split and the Opus fallback must be designed around for security or life-science workloads; 5.2 models require 30-day retention unless zero-data-retention is authorized.
AI-0026: What shipped: Google's top Gemini 4 model, released two weeks earlier only to cyber defenders in the Fairwind program, opened to paid Gemini API developers, enterprises (Gemini for business, Antigravity, CodeMender) and AI Ultra subscribers. Positioned above Argon for long-horizon agentic work, cybersecurity and open-ended research; it uses more tokens than Argon to reason and verify. Pricing: 2 in / 10 out per million through 2026-11-30, then 4 / 20. Vendor-reported: #1 on CursorBench 4.0, Perplexity WANDR and Zapier AutomationBench at more than 2x lower cost per task than the next external model; Gray Swan indirect-prompt-injection attack success 0%; 99% of simulated attack trajectories blocked; agentic honesty 92% (Argon 70%); no universal jailbreak found in a 132-hour external test. Also previewed: a /swarm multi-agent feature in Antigravity. Why it matters: the post-intro price is half the Fable 5.2 and GPT-6.2 Astra list price for a model that Anthropic's own table shows leading on AutomationBench; the injection result is vendor-measured on a static benchmark and should be read against the adaptive-attacker paper (AI-0067). Vertex AI availability was not stated on the page; see the Gemini Enterprise release notes (AI-0052).
AI-0027: What shipped: the mid-tier Gemini 4 model (gemini-4-neon), 1M context, four thinking levels with high as default and xhigh as maximum, available in the paid Gemini API, Gemini for business, Antigravity (where it is now the default) and the Gemini app for Pro and Ultra. Pricing 3 in / 0.15 cached / 15 out per million. Vendor-reported: Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index 61 at xhigh; Vals Index 70.9%; Agents' Last Exam v1.1 75.8%; Terminal-Bench Science 70.5%; Terminal-Bench 4.1 65.2%; FrontierCode 2.0 46.2%; Zapier AutomationBench 56.3% (#1); Vending-Bench 2 $16,843 (#1); SEC-bench Pro 90.5%; Gray Swan IPI 0.0%; Google claims 32% lower cost per task than Carbon at high. Why it matters: it completes a four-tier ladder (Hydrogen, Neon, Argon, Carbon) with one API and one 1M context, and Google explicitly pitches an orchestrator pattern where Carbon plans and cheaper tiers execute. Index positions are snapshots chosen by the vendor; cross-check on the live leaderboards before quoting them to a client.
AI-0028: What shipped: the fast tier of Gemini 4, replacing Gemini 3.8 Flash, available on all Gemini API tiers including free, in the Gemini app for free users, Google Search, Gemini for business and Sheets. 1M input and up to 1M output tokens; multimodal input (PDF, spreadsheets, charts, audio, video); flat pricing 1.50 in / 7.50 out per million across the whole context. Vendor-reported: Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index 51 at high (54 at xhigh); Terminal-Bench 4.1 57% versus 18.2% for 3.8 Flash; HLE-Diamond 58.8%; Vals Tax Agent Bench 52.3% (#1); Legal Research Bench 55.8%; Agents' Last Exam 71.6%; 2.5x faster task completion than 3.8 Flash. Why it matters: a free-tier model with a 1M output limit is a strong candidate for high-volume executor roles (extraction, document processing, tool execution) under a stronger planner, and its tax and legal benchmark placements are relevant to public-sector and financial clients. The page is inconsistent about whether its predecessor is 3.5 or 3.8 Flash, and no GA statement is made.
AI-0029: What shipped at Ignite 2026: a first-party model push positioned on price-performance rather than frontier capability. MAI Code 2 and MAI Code 2 Flash (in GitHub Copilot now; Flash in limited preview in Foundry), MAI Cyber 2 Flash (continuous codebase monitoring and patching), MAI Image 2.7 and 2.7 Flash (in Foundry), MAI Realtime 1 (speech to speech, interest form), Dragon Copilot Transcribe, Decision 1.1 (model-routing decision model, GA), the Maia 200 accelerator in production, and MAI Licensed Weights (coming soon via Frontier Company engagements): enterprises deploy and fine-tune MAI models inside their own Azure tenant, with Microsoft training on customer adaptations only by express agreement. Claims are relative and use promotional pricing: MAI Code 2 reaches 98% of GPT-6.1 Sol coding quality averaged over DeepSWE 1.1, Terminal Bench 2.1, SWE-Atlas and FrontierCode v1.1 at about 40% of the price (96% of Opus 5.5 at about 5%); Code 2 Flash comparable to GPT-6 Luna and Haiku 5.5 at a fraction of cost; MAI Cyber 2 Flash matches or beats GPT-6 Astra on CyberGym-E2E at under 2% of cost per task; Decision 1.1 is 50x faster and 79x cheaper than GPT-6.1 Sol. Microsoft says the Code models are not yet tuned for fundamental science or very long-horizon agentic work. Why it matters: for Azure-anchored clients this adds a cheaper first-party tier beneath OpenAI models in Copilot and Foundry, and Licensed Weights is a notable deployment model for data-residency-sensitive work. No absolute scores or list prices for most models were published.
AI-0030: Alibaba's first Qwen 4 model, proprietary (no weights), GA on the QwenCloud API, Qwen Studio, QwenWork and Qoder, with OpenAI- and Anthropic-compatible request formats, 1M context, text/image/video in, tool calling, structured output and batch. Pricing in the Singapore region 1.50 in / 4.50 out / 0.075 cached per million. Per VentureBeat's read of the official post: a 2.4T-parameter backbone with 71B active per token (figure unverified). Alibaba-reported: DeepSWE v1.1 75.7 (Opus 5.5 74.2, GPT-6.1 Sol 75.2), Terminal-Bench 4.0 48.5 (Kimi K3.1 67.2, Opus 5.5 59.6), AutomationBench-AA 72.5, Work360 52.69 at $1.67 per task. Ten-minute read.
AI-0055: An experimental MCP extension (io.modelcontextprotocol/files) for moving binary payloads without stuffing base64 into tool calls. Mechanism: a tool marks an argument with x-mcp-file in its input schema; a client may inline base64 under a server-declared maxInlineBytes, otherwise the server answers with an upload_required result carrying an upload URL and a single-use requestState; the client uploads over HTTPS (PUT or POST) and retries the call; downloads are delivered as _meta targets fetched with GET; a credentials option of omit or include is restricted to the MCP origin for include; clients must refuse redirects and targets that supply their own Authorization header; digests confirm integrity only. Status: draft with no reference implementation, finalization targeted before the end of 2026. Why it matters: document-heavy enterprise agents (PDF ingestion, report generation) need exactly this, and the security rules (single-use state, no redirects, origin-bound credentials) are the ones to require of any interim file-transfer design. Optional and may change.
AI-0056: Two consecutive security releases of the official MCP reference servers (v2.4.0 on 2026-11-11, v2.5.0 on 2026-11-18, after v2.3.0 on 11-04) fixed 14 GHSA-tracked issues: in the Git server, repository configuration that could make Git run programs (lazy fetch, auto-maintenance hooks, filter, merge and diff drivers, submodule config) and index entries pointing outside the working tree; in the filesystem server, symlink-swap directory escapes and time-of-check/time-of-use reads and moves; in the everything server, a NAT64 private-address bypass; in the fetch server, IPv6 site-local and robots.txt bypasses. Separately, Todoist's MCP server (CVE-2026-76807, CVSS 9.3) accepted browser-origin POSTs to its optional HTTP transport with no Host or Origin validation, enabling DNS-rebinding abuse of the stored API key (stdio unaffected; fixed in 10.3.3). A roundup also lists AWS MCP server bulletins (API MCP Server deny-list matching, Pricing MCP Server path traversal, a Timestream MCP token exfiltration) and a Kubernetes MCP server argument injection, from secondary sources. Caveats: some fixes are incomplete on Windows, and date-versioned npm packages will not auto-upgrade to the semver fixes. Why it matters: these servers are widely vendored into enterprise MCP stacks; inventory server versions, prefer stdio or authenticated HTTP with Origin checks, never auto-approve on annotations such as readOnlyHint, and scope credentials per server. Platform-side mitigations now appearing: Microsoft's MCP Firewall (AI-0044), AgentCore gateway interceptors and RCPs (AI-0046), Kiro's enforced sandboxing (AI-0053).
AI-0057: Dragos seeded roughly two million prompts between July and November 2026 with unique canary URLs, DNS names, AWS keys and other credentials across inference providers and routers, then watched for use. Findings: at least three hosting providers had request traffic copied by attackers, including one capture window that contained every request, even those rejected before model execution, which implies front-door interception rather than model-side logging; stolen AWS keys were used for tens of thousands of API calls (S3 listing, Secrets Manager and Parameter Store searches, Bedrock enablement attempts, IAM user creation); some stolen requests carried the zero-data-retention flag; marketplace resellers could read and retain prompts through ordinary logging; one router forwarded traffic to an undisclosed marketplace; a Chinese lab's systems fetched canary URLs from over half of the prompts sent to its models, including about two thirds flagged ZDR, and resellers of those models triggered the same scraper; one attacker used an LLM-driven pentest framework (ARTEX). OpenRouter responded on 2026-11-22: no breach of OpenRouter itself, three providers off-boarded, 125 endpoints removed from ZDR eligibility, customers notified, and ongoing canary-style verification before restoring ZDR; provider disclosures (per a CSA summary) describe a VM takeover at Phala, a credential committed by a coding agent at Together AI, and a routing misconfiguration at Novita. Dragos's recommendations: self-host the most sensitive work, use a first-tier provider with one contract, pin upstream providers and verify that privacy settings change routing, avoid reseller marketplaces, seed canary credentials in agent and pipeline context and treat any hit as an incident, enable provider secret filtering. Why it matters: router-level ZDR flags are contractual, not technical, controls; any enterprise using multi-provider routers should rotate every secret that ever appeared in a prompt and add canaries. The Together root cause is itself an agent-security lesson.
AI-0058: vLLM v0.34.0 (2026-11-16; 1,061 commits) removes Model Runner V1 so V2 is the only GPU runner, turns the extensible KV cache on by default (cache sized from free memory after warm-up, for example MiniMax-M3 on H200 from 433k to 672k tokens, at a 6 to 18% per-token decode latency cost at concurrency 128 on some models; opt out with --no-enable-extensible-kv-cache or --gpu-memory-utilization 0.9), changes the gpu_memory_utilization default to 1.0 and --block-size from 16 to 64, adds checkpoint and restore endpoints through CRIU and cuda-checkpoint, fault-tolerant data- and expert-parallel scale-down without restart, NUMA binding on by default, cache-aware admission (opt-in), a Rust frontend Responses API, and support for Mistral Large 4, MiniMax-M3.1-Flash, Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe and LFM3; it requires huggingface_hub 2.0 and removes several quantization paths. v0.33.0 (2026-11-02) moved to PyTorch 2.14, CUDA 13.0 only (12.9 artifacts dropped), ROCm 10.0, added a decisions endpoint, removed the Medusa and MLP speculators and the legacy Ray executor, and returns 503 during paused generation. Vendor-reported speedups include up to 1.95x decode on one model and 1.6x throughput on GLM-5.3-Flash. Why it matters: two consecutive releases with changed defaults and dropped CUDA versions; production operators must re-benchmark latency and re-pin container bases before upgrading, and older quantized checkpoints may break.
AI-0059: Hugging Face Transformers v5.22.0 to v5.24.0 (2026-10-29 to 11-21) added Mistral Large 4, FP8 adapter (LoRA/PEFT) training, Inkling 2 Small and Mini, LFM3, InternLM3, HY4-VL, EXAONE and others; v5.22.2 hardened the Jinja chat-template sandbox (a security patch) and v5.24.0 renamed past_key_values and cache_params to cache (compatibility until v5.40 for forward and v6.0 for generate) and requires peft 0.22; v5.21.0 introduced an FP8 backend for the quantized cache and new tensor-parallel embedding and expert-sharding plans (breaking), and v5.21.1 fixed a rope_scaling setter that broke remote-code loading in vLLM. AI-0061: Langfuse Cloud became v4-only on 2026-11-16: legacy batch ingestion endpoints, trace-level LLM-as-judge evaluators, deprecated read endpoints (traces, observations, sessions, scores, metrics, dataset runs) and the legacy export source were removed; Python SDK v2 and JS v3 or older stop ingesting, and Python v3 and JS v4 lose their querying API. AI-0062: Cerebras announced disaggregated inference in production (2026-11-17): GPUs (AMD Instinct in production) handle prompt processing (prefill) while Cerebras CS-3 systems handle output generation (decode), connected by KV Portal software that transfers intermediate model state over RDMA; partners can use the end-to-end stack (vLLM or SGLang for prefill plus Cerebras decode) or a decode-only SDK; early access for AWS, Fireworks AI, Gimlet Labs and General Compute. Vendor claim: five times more tokens per megawatt than CS-3-only on a GPT-OSS-120B endpoint. Why it matters: prefill/decode disaggregation is moving from a single-vendor GPU technique to heterogeneous hardware, and the serving research in the same window (Evolving Infra, AI-0071) shows agent workloads need runtime rebalancing of that split. Understand it as an inference-cost pattern rather than something to adopt now.
AI-0063: ServiceNow announced agentic continuous control monitoring in its Integrated Risk Management product (2026-11-10), integrated with its Super Intelligence Control Tower, with general availability expected in the first quarter of 2027: agents monitor compliance controls continuously instead of at audit time. Watchlist item: relevant to public-sector governance, risk and compliance clients once it ships; nothing to evaluate until the GA release and documentation exist.
AI-0064: Problem: long contexts dominate agent costs and later tokens cost more than earlier ones (up to 7x on frontier open-weight models per the paper), yet nobody had measured systematically how much long-horizon and long-input tasks actually need the history. Method: three regimes compared on the same models. Full-History Accumulation (baseline); End-of-Conversation Compaction (EoCC), where near a budget threshold the model writes a compact natural-language state (verbatim task, current intentions and next steps, artifacts needed to continue) and a fresh conversation resumes from task plus state; and Single-Action Compaction (SAC), where every step starts a new conversation from task plus state and performs exactly one action. Long-input tasks use selective reading plus compaction instead of stuffing documents into context. Results: on SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Multilingual, Terminal-Bench 2.1, FRAMES, tau2-bench and BFCLv3, Claude Opus 4.5 under EoCC stays within -3.7 to +5.6 points of baseline at 2.2x to 8.8x estimated savings and GPT 5.6 Sol within -3.3 to +4.4 at 2.4x to 5.0x; SAC holds too (Opus 4.5 70.2% versus 70.0% on SWE-bench Verified, 51.8% versus 47.2% on Terminal-Bench); on long-input suites (LongBench v2, LOONG, RULER, BABILong and others) compaction matched or beat baselines at 6.5x to 54.6x (Opus) and 4.4x to 233x (GPT) estimated savings. Open-weight models vary widely: Qwen 3 Coder Next fell from 53.0% to 3.6% at the tightest budget. The paper proposes semantic state space models: models post-trained to carry explicit natural-language state instead of a long context. Caveats: compaction is lossy by construction (a coin-toss counterexample), costs are modeled rather than billed, one table disagrees with the text on SAC median context, and SSSMs are proposed but not evaluated. Why it matters: the most actionable result of the window for agent cost control; set explicit context budgets in the tens of thousands of tokens with structured compaction, and validate per model before adopting with open weights.
AI-0065: Problem: do dedicated agent-memory systems beat retrieving directly from raw conversation history? Method: 11 memory systems (flat stores A-Mem, SimpleMem, MemOS; hierarchical or lifecycle systems MemoryOS, LightMem, OpenViking; graph systems HippoRAG2, PlugMem, MAGMA; trained policies Mem-T, Memory-R2) against 1-round and 2-round RAG over raw history plus no-, full- and gold-context baselines, on LongMemEval-s, a 20% subset of PersonaMem-v2 and a 10% subset of MINT-Eval, with three backbones (Qwen3.5-4B, Qwen3.6-27B, GPT-5.6 Luna at low effort), a shared embedding model and a shared LLM judge. Results: 90 of 99 system-benchmark-backbone configurations score below 2-round RAG; on LongMemEval-s all 33 lose, by 1.2 points (Mem-T) to 40.4 points (OpenViking on the 4B backbone); PersonaMem-v2 28 of 33 below; MINT-Eval 29 of 33 below. The paper decomposes net value into memory benefit (queries memory answers that RAG misses) and memory tax (queries RAG answers that memory loses because reorganization or distillation dropped or obscured evidence) and finds the tax dominates; gold-context replays show reorganized units lose exact phrasing and co-occurring details that questions need. Limitations: official configurations without per-system tuning, static offline English benchmarks, subsets used for cost, and no coverage of latent or parametric memory. Why it matters: before buying or building a memory layer, benchmark it against 2-round RAG over raw history on your own data; raw-history retrieval is also easier to audit and delete for regulated clients. Code and results are to be released on the project page.
AI-0066: Problem: indirect-injection benchmarks mostly test planted instructions that redirect the agent to a new task; real attacks can keep the task and its expected tools and tamper with a decision inside it. Contribution: an authority-based definition (planted content is an attack when it tries to influence a decision its source is not authorized to make) and a benchmark of 90 validated cases across Productivity, DevOps and Marketplace tool-use environments targeting six decision components (objective, decision rules, expected consequences, available actions, observation interpretation, world-state beliefs) plus compound cases. Evaluation: five models (DeepSeek V3.1, Kimi K2.5, Claude Sonnet 4 and 4.5, GLM-5) under seven defenses (Spotlighting, Sandwich, DRIFT-iso, DRIFT-full, Progent, CaMeL, ARGUS). Results (attack success rate, objective / rules / consequences / actions / observations / state / compound): no defense 15.0 / 21.2 / 13.7 / 19.0 / 12.4 / 18.6 / 21.8; DRIFT-iso 2.4 / 5.4 / 2.7 / 3.9 / 9.5 / 12.1 / 14.0; Progent 12.4 / 18.6 / 12.0 / 17.0 / 13.2 / 18.1 / 18.4; CaMeL 1.3 / 1.4 / 1.1 / 1.5 / 1.0 / 1.3 / 1.1; ARGUS 8.1 / 11.1 / 8.5 / 10.2 / 7.6 / 12.3 / 11.3. Detection-style defenses collapse objective attacks but leave observation and state tampering near 10%; tool-policy defenses barely help; capability-based data-flow control (CaMeL, where untrusted data cannot influence control flow) holds across all targets. Limitations: passive attacker, simulated environments with fictional records, environment-specific cases. Why it matters: the defenses that are easy to buy (content filters, tool allow-lists) fail against an attacker who corrupts what the agent believes about state or observations; the securing patterns in AI-0017 are the ones that held. Code and data are public.
AI-0067: Problem: static-payload injection research plateaued by mid-2025 and human red-teaming is saturating, yet models still reliably follow instructions in tool output when attacked by a capable agent. Method: an Agentic Optimizer of 8 teams of 2 agents, each with 20 evaluation calls (320 per scenario), coordinating through evaluation calls, team and global leaderboards and whiteboards, with a natural-language strategy database that can be frozen or updated from successful candidates; 100 Gemini-generated scenarios with random non-malicious goals, which isolates instruction-hierarchy robustness from security knowledge; defenders run with safety classifiers and out-of-model defenses disabled. Results (attack success at 150 defender queries / full budget, attacker Gemini 4 Argon): Gemini 3.6 Flash 97 / 99, 3.7 Flash 69 / 94, 3.8 Flash 66 / 90, Gemini 4 Argon 13 / 34, Kimi K3 95 / 99, GLM-5.3 99 / 99, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash 99 / 99; mean success at 150 queries rises from about 58 to 77 as the attacker model improves; against 80 AgentDojo scenarios it broke 7.5% versus 2.5% for a prior adaptive attacker at 25 defender queries. Limitations: synthetic goals, no deployed-stack defenses, a strategy database seeded by an older model, and an attacker third parties cannot reproduce (no code). Why it matters: a benchmark that says robust today is not evidence against an adaptive attacker with a few hundred queries; enterprise agent security must assume automated red-teaming and put defense in depth outside the model (capabilities, sandboxing, egress control, human approval for irreversible actions). Read it next to Gemini 4 Carbon's vendor-reported 0% static injection result (AI-0026).
AI-0068: Problem: does the interface through which identical capabilities are exposed change agent behavior? Method: MICA (Matched Interface Comparison and Analysis) renders both an MCP tool schema and a CLI from one shared action definition and runs them through the same runtime across six models and three interactive environments, producing paired trajectories with identical capability sets and a divergence analysis on action selection, failure handling and recovery; DART (Decoupled Action Realization and Targeted Repair) keeps validated semantic decisions and repairs the interface-specific execution step. Results: structured divergence in 94.3% of 2,004 paired episodes, with early differences propagating through later steps; DART improves the benchmark score in all six settings by up to 9.0 points and reduces MCP token cost in all three environments by up to 27.1k tokens per task. What is new: the first controlled, capability-matched comparison that treats the interface representation as part of the environment rather than a neutral wrapper. Limitations: affiliations and per-environment numbers could not be verified from the abstract page, no public code, only three environments. Why it matters for MCP architecture decisions: schema shape, naming and error surfaces measurably change outcomes and cost, so tool-surface design deserves the same evaluation discipline as prompts; consider composable CLI-style tools for some workflows and read Anthropic's tool-writing guidance alongside it.
AI-0069: Problem: prior environment-scaling pipelines synthesize a database first and derive tools and tasks from it, producing unrealistic tool interfaces, compositions not grounded in execution and single-environment tasks. Method: ToolSpace reverses the order. It mines data, state and retry dependencies between adjacent calls in real MCP execution traces with deterministic rules, clusters the dependency graph into environments, synthesizes databases only for state-mutating environments, runs state-aware random walks with rollback to build tool chains, converts each chain into a natural-language task with assertion checks, and keeps only samples that replay successfully from the initial state; the result is used for supervised fine-tuning, optionally followed by agent RL. It also introduces harder Pro versions of AutomationBench and tau3-Bench Banking on which seven frontier models drop by up to 38.2 points. Results on a seven-benchmark average (AutomationBench, SkillsBench, JobBench, tau3-Bench Banking, BFCL V4, Harvey LAB, OfficeQA Pro): Qwen3.6-35B-A3B 23.0 to 41.0 (43.2 with RL), with AutomationBench 8.2 to 45.8; a GLM-5.2 backbone 44.6 to 56.6, matching Claude Opus 5 (56.6) and above Qwen 3.8 Max, GLM 5.3, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Kimi K3 and GPT 5.6 Sol; at 8B it beats Agent-Reflex and Agent-World baselines by about 10 points; execution-witnessed dependencies beat LLM-judged ones and gains scale with data and environment count. Limitations: work in progress, no limitations section, small Pro benchmarks (300 and 98 tasks), some baselines reproduced locally, no code listed. Why it matters: an enterprise running its own MCP servers can turn real traces into training environments and bring a mid-size open model near frontier on its own tool-use tasks.
AI-0070: Problem: code-search benchmarks show dense encoders beating BM25, yet coding agents thrive on grep. Method: Repo-Premium, a preregistered file-ranking benchmark built from 2022 to 2026 pull requests in more than 91 repositories across six languages with curated and raw queries; 13 dense checkpoints from six families (jina-code-embeddings-0.5b as canonical, Qwen3-Embedding, C2LLM, F2LLM, E5, gte-Qwen2) plus SPLADE and ColBERTv2, against BM25 at 1,000-character chunks, whole-file tuned BM25, IDF-weighted grep, and generate-then-grep (whole-file BM25 over a query expanded with LLM-written identifiers). Results (nDCG@10, source-file labels): curated pre-cutoff queries dense 0.532 versus whole-file BM25 0.498 versus BM25 plus generated anchors 0.613; raw post-cutoff 0.597 / 0.539 / 0.651; the dense premium over chunked BM25 is +0.121 but shrinks to +0.034 against whole-file BM25; dense still gains 0.10 to 0.19 Recall@10; reciprocal-rank fusion reaches 0.609 versus 0.550 dense-only on the development pool; per-query routing never beat fixed fusion. The paper attributes much of the reported dense advantage to evaluation choices (chunking files for BM25, counting edited tests as relevant) and to queries lacking rare identifiers. Limitations: ten Python repositories form the core set with one repository per other language, BM25 tuned on evaluation queries, file-level labels only, localization rather than fix correctness. Why it matters: for code RAG the default should be hybrid BM25 plus dense with LLM query expansion; pure dense may be paying for an evaluation artifact. The dataset is public on Hugging Face.
AI-0071: Problem: prefill/decode-disaggregated serving adapts poorly to agentic workloads at runtime, causing load imbalance between phases and evicting KV caches that agents reuse across branches. Method: symmetric engines on every node can serve either phase and switch at runtime (6.2 s average versus a 754 s Dynamo relaunch), with KV cache in a shared host-memory pool and a cluster-wide directory counting active-branch references per block; an online planner learns prefill and decode iteration-time models without offline profiling and resizes the split only when the predicted gain is statistically robust; an agent-aware KV manager evicts zero-reference blocks first, routes to the prefill node with the shortest predicted time to first token, and prefetches remote KV asynchronously while requests queue. Results on 36 GB300 GPUs (scaling to 256, with a 3,072-GPU simulation) using GLM-5.2 on PutnamBench and replayed Claude Code traces and Kimi K2.6 on OSWorld 2.0, against Dynamo 1.5.1, the best static SGLang split, SGLang Model Gateway with HiCache and a reimplemented Arrow: 1.10 to 2.73x throughput, 1.15 to 4.12x lower mean end-to-end latency, up to 13.92x lower P95 time to first token and 81 to 95% less lost KV reuse versus Dynamo; up to 38% more throughput than the best static split at stationary load; 2.14x throughput under a workload composition shift; online adaptation costs 0.3% throughput. Limitations: Arrow reimplemented, large-scale numbers simulated, headline multipliers differ slightly between sections. Why it matters: platform teams serving coding or computer-use agents on disaggregated clusters should expect to need runtime rebalancing and branch-aware KV eviction; the KV-reuse signal from agent context management is the transferable idea. Code is public.
AI-0072: Google's open embedding model for text, image, audio, video and mixtures, built for resource-constrained deployment. Architecture: a 744M full model (271M backbone, 167M vision encoder, 305M audio encoder) with text-only 271M, vision-language 439M and audio-language 577M configurations via selective encoder loading, simplified per-layer embeddings, a multi-stage curriculum that introduces modalities gradually, Matryoshka truncation to 768, 512, 256 or 128 dimensions, int4 quantization-aware checkpoints and an adjustable vision token budget. Results: MTEB Multilingual v2 61.36 (Jina Embed v5 Omni Nano 65.52, Qwen3 Embed 0.6B 64.34); MTEB English v2 68.46 (a slight regression from 69.67); MTEB Code 78.68 (Qwen3 75.42, within two points of a model about 28x larger); MMEB-v2 59.01; MIEB lite 60.17; MSEB audio retrieval 69.54 with native audio versus 50.95 for the previous model via speech recognition; on-device memory on a Pixel 11 Pro 191 MB text-only, 447 MB with vision, 567 MB full. Limitations: English text slightly worse than v1, weak speaker clustering, specialist audio-text models still better on captioning retrieval, some comparisons use different harnesses. Why it matters: one small open model for multimodal RAG and on-device search, and the code-retrieval score and quantized footprints are the deployment-relevant numbers; a reasonable default embedding for on-premises pipelines. Model weights are on Hugging Face.
AI-0073: A taxonomy from Microsoft Security Response Center, UNSW and ETH Zurich for prompt injection attacks along nine dimensions: source label, fragmentation, presentation visibility, instruction interpretability, conditionality, agent-state modification, topic relation to the task, intended effect, and whether the original task still completes. The authors use it to audit nine benchmarks (AgentDojo, IPIArena, LLMail-Inject, WASP, AgentPI, DualView, Sleeper Memory, Trojan Hippo, StepJack) and six real incidents (a GitHub MCP exfiltration, a hidden-Unicode skill, terminal DNS exfiltration, an obfuscated Claude Computer Use command, M365 Copilot memory poisoning, a Devin port exposure) and find that 13% of pairwise category combinations are untested anywhere. Why it matters: when choosing or building injection defenses, this is a coverage checklist that reveals which attack classes a vendor's benchmark never exercised; combine with the task-tampering results (AI-0066) and the adaptive-attacker results (AI-0067) for a realistic threat model.
AI-0074: Problem: decision models (typed single-pass outputs such as a choice with a probability instead of generated text; JEV is the earliest public one, closed and API-only) have been judged mainly as actors. Method: separate three roles, actor, judge and teacher, and compare three decision models (JEV, Decider v1.2, GPT Decisions) with three general-LLM configurations on ALFWorld as actors and post-episode judges, then use JEV per-action scores as rewards to train a Qwen2.5-1.5B policy with GRPO on ALFWorld and WebShop. Results: as actors JEV reaches 42.9% and Decider 63.6% on ALFWorld, and all six configurations collapse on ordered-subgoal tasks (JEV 70.8% unordered versus at most 18.8% ordered); as a judge, with the full trajectory JEV's mean score for contributing actions rises from 0.41 to 0.59 and the question did this action help separates useful from no-op actions by 0.36 versus 0.05; as a teacher, GRPO with JEV rewards lifts the 1.5B policy from 72.8% to 82.9% on ALFWorld and 56.8% to 71.4% on WebShop, beating a 7B policy trained with GRPO alone (77.6% and 66.1%) for about 22 to 30 dollars of teacher API cost. Limitations: two text environments, episodes of at most 30 actions, judges only score after episode end, closed models prevent attribution. Why it matters: a cheap typed reward and judge signal for agent RL and for post-hoc trajectory auditing, and a caution against using decision models as the action-selecting brain for ordered multi-step tasks. Code is public.
AI-0075: A pre-window preprint (2026-09-29) surfaced through reports of strong ICLR 2027 reviews: Context Language Models let the model edit its own context as a file rather than accumulating tokens, with reported gains of +11.4% accuracy on BrowseComp-Plus at 21.5% fewer FLOPs and a Suffix Cache Reuse technique claiming 35% less server compute than SGLang. Reported affiliation is University of Washington with Meta FAIR; OpenReview scores could not be verified because of a verification wall, so treat the review signal as hearsay and the arXiv paper as the source. Why it matters: it is the model-side counterpart to the compaction results in AI-0064 and to context-engineering practice (notes, compaction, just-in-time retrieval); if the ICLR decision on 2026-12-16 confirms it, it becomes a P1 read for how future models will manage context natively.
AI-0076: Problem: is context rot in retrieval caused by raw length or by competition for attention? Method: a single hidden key-value evidence statement placed at a fixed depth, scored by query log-probability, under four length-matched conditions (short, neutral filler, competing statements from 51 keys, masked filler), with loss defined as the log ratio of short-context to condition probability and attention mass on the evidence recorded from eight selected heads, across five small models (Qwen2.5 0.5B and 1.5B, SmolLM2 1.7B, OLMo-2 1B, Llama-3.2-3B base) and 126,473 trials, with code and all trial-level measurements released. Results: neutral filler keeps accuracy at 0.97 to 1.00 up to 32K tokens on Qwen2.5-1.5B while evidence-formatted competitors drop it to 0.16 to 0.33; one rival value for the queried key multiplies loss by 9 to 110x; attention mass on the evidence explains up to 58% of loss variance versus at most 8% for log length; the masked-filler protocol that claims length alone hurts reproduces on MMLU but masking itself costs 45 points at 32K while the same filler left visible costs nothing. Limitations: models of 3B parameters or fewer, a predictive rather than causal attention measure, a single synthetic task, non-preregistered conflict analysis. Why it matters for RAG: degradation comes from packing near-duplicate or conflicting chunks together, so deduplication and conflict handling matter more than simply shrinking context; read with Lost in the Middle (AI-0009) and Context Rot (AI-0010).
AI-0077: Turn-level credit assignment for multi-turn agent RL. Multiscale Advantage Estimation sums temporal-difference residuals within each turn, applies GAE across turns to get a turn-level advantage, computes a centered within-turn local trace, and combines them (beta = 0 reduces to broadcasting the turn advantage); the policy update uses turn-level importance sampling, and an ablation with token-level importance sampling shows the scale alignment matters. Results on Qwen3-4B-Thinking and Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct: BrowseComp-Plus 48.08 / 50.32, GAIA 39.47 / 43.42, Claw-Eval pass@3 66.91 / 73.22, AutomationBench 13.33 / 15.00, claimed best on nine metrics against GRPO, GSPO, PPO, VAPO and SAO; GiGPO is cited but not compared and each setting has a single run. Code is public under the IQuestLab organization; affiliations were not verifiable. A drop-in estimator to try if you run multi-turn agent RL.
AI-0078: A 67-page CMU, JHU and Aurora paper arguing that the pretrain, midtrain, SFT and RL stage split is not fundamental: for binary rewards the gradient of log success probability equals the expected policy gradient under the success-conditioned policy, so a MaxRL update is maximum likelihood on that policy held fixed, and all stages collapse into one likelihood loss over a time-varying mixture of static corpora and RL-generated samples. Experiments at 124M (20B pretraining tokens, Reasoning-Gym puzzles) and 0.76B (240M-token mixed midtraining, RL on Math12K, evaluated on MATH-500, GSM8K, HumanEval+, MBPP+, SciQ, ARC-C, MMLU) show the best unified configurations beating staged training on several settings, better accuracy-compute trade-offs at large and very small budgets, better retention of held-out pretraining loss and general benchmarks, and higher final coding accuracy in continual learning. Limitations: small scale, one RL task at a time, no scaling laws, preliminary MaxRL comparison. Mostly conceptual today; the continual-learning retention result is the one to watch for enterprise fine-tuning that must avoid forgetting. Skim sections 1 to 3.
AI-0079: LoCo targets the local stop-or-continue decision in reasoning models instead of whole-trajectory compression, using only the model's own math traces: score each step under the next-token distribution and flag low-confidence, high-volatility steps; a Qwen3-30B judge labels flagged steps as overthinking, normal or final; freeze the prefix at confirmed overthinking points, sample eight continuations and keep the shortest correct one; train with DPO on (long, short-verified) pairs. On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B: MATH-500 91.88 to 91.80 with 44.1% fewer tokens, AIME24 50.83 to 54.17 at -45.4%, AIME25 37.92 to 40.42 at -45.2%, LiveCodeBench 41.77 to 42.51 at -24.7%, CodeContests 18.48 to 20.61 at -23.4%; math-only training transfers to code; baselines DAST and TokenSqueeze either compress less or lose accuracy. One 7B base, no limitations section, external judge in data construction. A cheap self-distillation recipe to cut 25 to 45% of reasoning tokens from an open reasoning model. Code is public.
AI-0080: Tool observations are compressed into latent tokens in the agent's embedding space with action-preserving training, so the agent conditions on a compact representation instead of the raw text of tool output. Reported: 70.01 to 89.24% fewer tokens and 24.45 to 55.97% lower runtime with improved QA accuracy across four benchmarks. Relevance: a model-side alternative to the prompt-side compaction in AI-0064 for the specific cost of verbose tool results; applicable only where you control the model and can train the compressor. Code is public under the THU-Agent organization.
AI-0081: Defines an empirical mismatch budget for on-policy distillation: how much training-inference mismatch (quantized or asynchronous rollouts) the method tolerates before quality drops. Findings: FP8 rollout recipes give at least 1.93x the KV-cache tokens of BF16, FP8 plus asynchronous rollouts reach equal quality 1.62x sooner, and on-policy distillation stays stable where reinforcement learning destabilizes under the same mismatch. Relevance: if you distill a large model into a smaller deployable one, cheaper low-precision and asynchronous rollouts are acceptable within a measurable budget. Code is public.
AI-0082: RepoFactory scales long-horizon coding-agent training by turning real repositories into 10,159 verifiable repository-building environments across 17 domains through an Environment Evolution Loop. Training Qwen3.5-35B-A3B on them produces RepoHorizen-35B-A3B with a 22.6-point gain on NL2Repo-Bench (17.5 without the evolution loop) and +8.5 average across five benchmarks. Part of the theme that training environments, not model weights, are the scarce asset for agent capability; pairs with ToolSpace (AI-0069).
AI-0083: DICE makes speculative decoding less speculative: it pre-samples and synchronizes the verification randomness so that draft-tree node selection and next-round prefetching target the continuations that will actually be accepted, reporting speedups of up to 24.6 percentage points over strong baselines with no drafter retraining and an exact target distribution. Relevance: a serving-side latency gain you get from the engine, not from model choice; watch for adoption in vLLM or SGLang before acting.
AI-0084: Problem: W4A16 quantized agents often ignore task requirements or environment state and diverge from successful full-precision runs. Method: a full-precision teacher steers the quantized student to revise failed turns, the revision is executed and verified, and the student is trained to reproduce the corrected behavior at corrected turns and the teacher elsewhere. Results (W4A16 averages over BFCL V4, tau2-Bench, WebShop, ALFWorld, Search QA): Qwen3-8B 53.18 versus BF16 53.54 and QeRL 51.00; Qwen3.5-4B 60.95 versus 61.68; Gemma 4 12B 64.31 versus 65.13; +1.84 points over QeRL on tau2-Bench with 67% fewer training GPU hours. Models of 12B or smaller, no code. Relevance: quantized small agents for on-premises or edge deployment can recover near-full-precision task success; pair with Jagged Robustness (AI-0087) because safety does not transfer evenly under quantization.
AI-0085: Clover-35B-A3B-Preview from DiffuSpace is a mixture-of-experts block-diffusion language model (35B total, 3B active) with Gated-DeltaNet memory and in-block bidirectional attention, released under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. The vendor-reported numbers (SWE-bench Verified 73.6, Terminal-Bench 2.1 51.7, 680 tokens per second on a single GB300 at batch 1) would make it the first diffusion LLM with credible agentic-coding capability. Watchlist: independent validation is needed before drawing conclusions; the non-commercial licence limits enterprise use.
AI-0086: Reflection's technical report for Beam, a 501.3B-total / 23.4B-active mixture-of-experts model trained on 23.8T tokens with a 1M context, asynchronous RL on 10.5K GB300 GPUs with more than 100M rollouts over about four weeks, served in FP8 and NVFP4 with a 1.93B DFlash 2 drafter; reported safety behavior refuses or pivots 88.9% of harmful requests and complies with 81.5% of harmless ones; 229 authors, CC BY-SA 4.0 report. A weights link was not on the abstract page. Useful mainly as a transparent frontier-scale training recipe to compare against vendor claims.
AI-0087: On Qwen3-4B, quantization degrades safeguards and bias unevenly while truthfulness holds, and universal adversarial suffixes that are harmless on the full-precision model jailbreak the quantized one. Numbers are in the paper rather than the abstract. Practical rule: re-run safety and red-team evaluations after quantizing, not just capability benchmarks. Code is public.
AI-0088: A bootstrap non-inferiority test for replacing a human annotator with an LLM judge when items lack shared annotators, evaluated over 18 LLMs, five prompting techniques and 20 datasets: LLMs pass in about half of the setups, and about 100 items suffice for the test. Relevance: a statistical gate you can put in front of LLM-as-judge adoption in an evaluation pipeline, instead of assuming agreement.
AI-0089: A meta-study of 40 technical reports for open-weight LLMs: only 19 of 73 novelty claims have a with-and-without ablation, 4 of 40 reports state more than one training run, and 1 of 40 discloses data mixture, token count and compute together. Relevance: calibrates how much weight to give vendor technical reports when evaluating models; ask for the ablation before accepting an architectural claim.
